nodes.name: L1: a member that is better alone does not predict stack weight

Gate: say what information the stack lacks that this adds; stack read on folds 0+4 before any further fold. Reconsider when residual correlation with the stack is below 0.9.

nodes.name: L2: a folds 0+4 gain is a screen, never quoted as a gain

nodes.source: docs/LANES_20261108.md 'Shared ledger, decision ids, lessons, verifier' (PI approved as rules 2026-11-11; wording and numbers are the coordinator's); docs/FRAMEWORK_REVISION_20261111.md section 3; shared notes ledger_20261111.jsonl L2

nodes.name: L3: read a one-seed gain with the seed mean before adoption

nodes.name: L4: quote the strictly nested value with the as-computed value next to it

nodes.name: L6: name convention, folds and baseline of both numbers; recompute the incumbent in the same run

nodes.title: Test-time Adaptation for Regression by Subspace Alignment
nodes.citation: Adachi K, Yamaguchi S, Kumagai A, Hamagami T. Test-time Adaptation for Regression by Subspace Alignment. ICLR 2025. arXiv:2410.03263
nodes.tldr: Source-free TTA for regression (SSA): store mean/covariance of penultimate features, project onto the top-K PCA subspace, weight directions by their effect on the regressor, and align target features with a symmetric KL by updating only normalisation-layer affine parameters; classification TTA methods (BN-adapt, prototypes, feature restoration, TTT) often HURT regression.
nodes.relevance_note: The one TTA method designed for regression heads like ours; also a warning that plain BN-statistics adaptation can sharply reduce R2, relevant to our two image sources and the HEX OOF-to-test gap.
nodes.data_scale: SVHN->MNIST digit regression, UTKFace age with 13 ImageNet-C corruptions, Biwi Kinect head pose (gender shift), California Housing (non-coastal->coastal)
key_numbers: UTKFace mean over 13 corruptions R2: source -0.678, BN-adapt 0.654, feature restoration 0.700, SSA 0.731, oracle 0.789 (verified-from-source)
California Housing R2: source 0.605, BN-adapt 0.318, prototype -0.726, SSA 0.639 (verified-from-source)
Biwi Kinect R2: source 0.706, BN-adapt 0.746, feature restoration -0.357, TTT 0.288, SSA 0.778 (verified-from-source)
SVHN->MNIST R2: source 0.406, BN-adapt 0.396, SSA 0.511; naive all-dimension alignment 0.333 (verified-from-source)
Defaults: K=100 PCA dims of 2048-d features, batch 64, one offline epoch over target data; K>=400 unstable on SVHN-MNIST (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: Before any test-time BN re-estimation on new/darker frames, check on the old-vs-new source split (CD MAPE 7.11 vs 5.50) whether BN-adapt helps or hurts; if TTA is allowed, try SSA (K about 100, affine-only updates) on the regression heads and measure per-source OOF MAPE, especially HEX.

compares_with.note: Tent/entropy methods not evaluated because they need class probabilities

has_limitation.note: Assumes covariate shift only (p(y|x) unchanged); diagonal-Gaussian feature assumption may not hold
Sensitive to K (large K diverges); offline epoch over target data with batch 64
No medical or microscopy data; label-noise and device-label shift (our device computes CV differently) would violate the covariate-shift assumption

nodes.title: Segment Anything for Microscopy
nodes.citation: Archit A, Freckmann L, Nair S, Khalid N, Hilt P, Rajashekar V, et al. Segment Anything for Microscopy. Nat Methods. 2025;22(3):579-591. doi:10.1038/s41592-024-02580-4
nodes.tldr: micro-sam fine-tunes SAM for light and electron microscopy, adds an automatic instance segmentation (AIS) decoder predicting centre/boundary distances + foreground with seeded watershed, and a napari tool for interactive annotation and fine-tuning; automatic quality is on par with Cellpose on LIVECell.
nodes.relevance_note: Alternative SAM-based base model; its gains come from annotation-based fine-tuning and interactive correction, which our no-manual-annotation rule forbids; no label-free adaptation is discussed.
nodes.data_scale: LM generalist: LIVECell, DeepBacs, TissueNet, NeurIPS CellSeg, PlantSeg root, DSB, StarDist set, 8 Cell Tracking Challenge datasets (counts in Suppl. Table 1, not read)

has_limitation.note: Automatic segmentation only on par with Cellpose; does not claim superiority; poor automatic results on Lizard and mouse embryo
Adaptation path assumes manual/interactive labels; no pseudo-label or label-free mode

nodes.title: Automatic determination of endothelial cell density from donor cornea endothelial cell images
nodes.citation: Benetz BAM, Shivade VS, Joseph NM, Romig NJ, McCormick JC, Chen J, et al. Automatic determination of endothelial cell density from donor cornea endothelial cell images. Transl Vis Sci Technol. 2024;13(8):40. doi:10.1167/tvst.13.8.40
nodes.tldr: On US eye-bank donor images (Konan CellChek D), a self-supervised ViT/UNETR border segmenter estimated ECD with bias 123 cells/mm2 on the whole image but only 46 when restricted to a region matched to the area the eye bank counted (Lin's rc 0.77 vs 0.88); bias grew with ECD.
nodes.relevance_note: Closest published analogue of CLEAR-EC (US eye banks, Konan CellChek D, technician-counted region); shows that matching the technician's region roughly halves-to-thirds the CD bias.
nodes.data_scale: 15,138 unlabelled images (8,169 donors) for SSL; 174 labelled; 3,024 test images, 1,939 with >= 100 cells by both methods
key_numbers: Whole image: manual 2730 +- 349 vs automated 2607 +- 272 cells/mm2; bias 123 (95 % CI 114-131); Lin's rc 0.77; LoA -234 to 479; 81 % within 10 % (verified-from-source)
Cropped to region matched to the eye-bank counted area: automated 2683 +- 277; bias 46 (39-53); Lin's rc 0.88; LoA -243 to 335; 93 % within 10 % (verified-from-source)
Bias grew by about 134 (whole) and 120 (cropped) cells/mm2 per 500 cells/mm2 of ECD (verified-from-source)
Automated method found 100-1,263 cells per image vs 100-371 for manual counting (verified-from-source)
CV and HEX not reported (beyond scope) (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: For CD, compute the point-based density only inside a predicted technician region (the densest, most legible window of about 17 % of the frame) and add a slope term that grows with density (their bias rose about 25 % of ECD per 500 cells/mm2), fitted on OOF MAPE.
search_keywords: donor cornea endothelial cell density deep learning eye bank

has_limitation.note: CV and HEX were beyond the study's scope.
Manual eye-bank analysis procedure is not described beyond >= 40 (ideally > 100) cells; the cropped region was matched in area, not in location, to what technicians counted.

nodes.title: Improving 3D deep learning segmentation with biophysically motivated cell synthesis
nodes.citation: Bruch R, Vitacolonna M, Nurnberg E, Sauer S, Rudolf R, Reischl M. Improving 3D deep learning segmentation with biophysically motivated cell synthesis. Commun Biol. 2025;8. doi:10.1038/s42003-025-07469-2
nodes.tldr: Cell geometries from a Cellular Potts simulation, rendered by an imaging simulation (PSF, brightness loss, noise) plus CycleGAN refinement, train a 3D StarDist that beats training on 37.5 h of manual annotation (SEG 0.534 vs 0.505); direct GAN label-to-image translation looks realistic but fails (label inconsistency).
nodes.relevance_note: Best recent sim-to-real recipe for tessellated tissue: simulate geometry with measured shape statistics, render with a physical imaging model, refine with CycleGAN; warns that pure GAN translation breaks label consistency.
nodes.data_scale: one HT-29 spheroid recording; 4 synthetic training volumes per method; 3 manually corrected test patches with 1001 nuclei
key_numbers: SEG / DET: SimOptiGAN+ (biophysical placement) 0.534 / 0.800 vs manual-annotation training 0.505 / 0.785 vs pretrained Cellpose nuclei 0.332 / 0.512 (verified-from-source)
Upper bound (trained on test data) 0.593 / 0.891 (verified-from-source)
Direct unpaired label-to-image GAN (Mem2NucGAN-U) 0.103 / 0.155 despite lowest KID (verified-from-source)
Manual annotation cost 37.5 h vs 0.4-4.4 h for synthetic pipelines (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: If we build synthetic endothelium for CV/HEX pretraining, render geometry with an explicit imaging model fit to our frames (Gaussian PSF/blur, dark cell borders, vignetting and brightness falloff like the 2023-24 images, noise) and use a GAN only as a light refinement; do not rely on unpaired label-to-image GAN alone, which can break the geometry the label depends on.

has_limitation.note: Single spheroid/cell line; manual work still needed for parameters and prototypes; performance may drop for different morphology or density
3D fluorescence nuclei, not 2D specular endothelium; transfer of the recipe is by analogy

nodes.title: Simulation of specular microscopy images of corneal endothelium, a tool for control of measurement errors
nodes.citation: Bucht C, Soderberg P, Manneberg G. Simulation of specular microscopy images of corneal endothelium, a tool for control of measurement errors. Acta Ophthalmol. 2011;89(3):e242-e250. doi:10.1111/j.1755-3768.2010.01974.x
nodes.tldr: A simulator generates specular-microscopy-like endothelium images with preset mean and variation of cell structure and stores exact per-cell morphometry; analysing simulated images with Topcon imagenet-640 revealed a scaling error in the software's cell-size-variation (CV) estimate and an operator-dependent random error.
nodes.relevance_note: Direct precedent that a Topcon device's CV is a scaled version of true CV; matches our fact that device CV is about twice the Voronoi area CV, and offers a synthetic-image route to calibrate that mapping.
nodes.data_scale: several hundred simulated images over the physiological ECD range; 12 analysed with imagenet-640 by one operator
key_numbers: Simulator stores exact per-cell morphometry; image quality varied with a filter toolbox (from-abstract)
Several hundred unique images generated; 12 selected evenly over the physiological ECD range for the error study (from-abstract)
imagenet-640 estimates of cell size variation show a scaling error vs true simulated values; random error strongly operator-dependent (from-abstract)
Slope / intercept of the scaling error: not reported in what was read (from-abstract)

results.task: device CV vs true CV on simulated images
results.metric: regression of software estimate on truth
results.value: scaling error present (size not in abstract)

nodes.suggests_try: Treat device CV as a scaled (and possibly offset) function of true area CV: fit a per-source linear/isotonic map from a segmentation-robust CV estimate (expert-marker or detector-based) to device CV on OOF and apply it before blending, rather than asking the network to learn the scale implicitly; widen predicted CV spread accordingly.

has_limitation.note: Only the abstract was accessible (Wiley 403; full text exists as a PDF on an Uppsala site, not fetched under the no-download rule); slope of the scaling error and simulator algorithm unverified

nodes.title: CLEAR-EC: Corneal Learning for Endothelial Assessment and Review using AI for Endothelial Count (challenge site, dataset record and baseline)
nodes.citation: Al-Aswad L, Liang P, Huang Z, Eye-Bank for Sight Restoration, AltruVision (Lions Eye Bank), The Eye Bank of Kentucky, Georgia Eye Bank. CLEAR-EC: Corneal Learning for Endothelial Assessment and Review using AI for Endothelial Count [dataset]. Zenodo; 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.21270595
nodes.tldr: Public pages state the task, metric and data origin (9,000 training + 1,000 test specular images from US eye banks in NY, GA, KY, DE) but not which device or analysis mode produced the CD/CV/HEX labels; the baseline is Cellpose v1 'cyto' plus per-cell morphology in a random 40 % x 40 % crop.
nodes.relevance_note: Primary source for what the organisers say about labels: nothing about the device algorithm is published; KONAN is named only as an example of the eye-bank workflow.
nodes.data_scale: 9,000 training + 1,000 test images (BMP, about 1.5-2 MB); Phase I 100 test images, Phase II 1,000
key_numbers: Score: per-metric mean absolute percent error |pred - gt| / gt x 100, equal-weight mean of CD, CV, HEX (verified-from-source)
9,000 training and 1,000 test images from eye banks in New York, Georgia, Kentucky and Delaware (verified-from-source)
Phase I: 100 test images, up to 3 runs; Phase II: 1,000 test images, up to 2 runs; Phase II Oct 1 - Nov 14 (verified-from-source)

Baseline pixel size fixed at 1000/1296 um per pixel; CD = N x 1e6 / total area; CV = std/mean area; baseline HEX = mean IoU of each cell with a fitted hexagon (not the six-sided share) (verified-from-source)
Device and label-generation procedure: not reported on any public page (verified-from-source)

has_limitation.note: No published description of how labels were produced (device model, center vs flex-center vs auto, technician protocol); no challenge paper; Phase I/II algorithm descriptions are behind sign-in and were not read.

nodes.title: Automated segmentation of the corneal endothelium in a large set of 'real-world' specular microscopy images using the U-Net architecture
nodes.citation: Daniel MC, Atzrodt L, Bucher F, Wacker K, Bohringer S, Reinhard T, Bohringer D. Automated segmentation of the corneal endothelium in a large set of 'real-world' specular microscopy images using the U-Net architecture. Sci Rep. 2019;9:4752. doi:10.1038/s41598-019-41034-2
nodes.tldr: U-Net trained on watershed labels grown from expert centroid dots in 385 Topcon SP-3000 images finds only 34 % of cells (precision 0.84) yet estimates ECD with R2 0.96 vs manual, because ECD is taken as the inverse median Voronoi area of the detected cells.
nodes.relevance_note: This 385-image Topcon centroid set appears to be the external point set our detector was trained on; it shows density from the median Voronoi area of a confident subset is robust to very low recall.
nodes.data_scale: 385 Topcon SP-3000 images from 385 patients (158 gradable train, 227 validation), expert centroid dots
key_numbers: 385 images, 260 x 476 px, digitised from analog video prints; median 90 dotted cells per image (verified-from-source)
U-Net recall 0.34, precision 0.84 on centroids (8 px tolerance) (verified-from-source)
ECD R2 vs manual 0.96 (U-Net) vs 0.35 (marker-driven watershed); 92 % of images within +/-250 cells/mm2, 99 % within +/-500 (verified-from-source)
61 images ungradable by experts; U-Net flagged 92 as ungradable (verified-from-source)
CV and HEX not reported (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: For CD, replace count-based density with 1/median(Voronoi area) (or median nearest-neighbour spacing) over only high-confidence detections in the label box; this paper got R2 0.96 at recall 0.34, so our 15 % misses should barely matter for CD if we use robust local spacing rather than counts.

has_limitation.note: Low recall caused by removing objects under 1000 px; single rater per image; single center/device
No CV/HEX evaluation; images are digitised analog prints, older than CLEAR-EC frames

nodes.title: Mind the gap: Performance metric evaluation in brain-age prediction
nodes.citation: de Lange AMG, Anatürk M, Rokicki J, Han LKM, Franke K, Alnæs D, et al. Mind the gap: Performance metric evaluation in brain-age prediction. Hum Brain Mapp. 2022;43(10):3113-3129. doi:10.1002/hbm.25837
nodes.tldr: Regression predictions are always biased toward the training mean when the input-target relation is imperfect; 'age-bias corrections' that use the true target make even poor models look accurate, while the label-free slope correction just inflates prediction variance.
nodes.relevance_note: Our CV predictions span 66 % of the label spread at r 0.686; this paper says that compression is the normal signature of an imperfect regressor and that label-free de-shrinking inflates variance rather than fixing error.
nodes.data_scale: UK Biobank N = 37,156; Cam-CAN N = 622 (T1 MRI, 10-fold CV)
key_numbers: UKB, 10-fold CV: r 0.728 -> 0.898, R2 0.529 -> 0.760, MAE 4.140 -> 2.969 years after age-bias correction that uses chronological age (verified-from-source)
Cam-CAN: r 0.870 -> 0.927, R2 0.753 -> 0.837, MAE 7.403 -> 6.001 years after the same correction (verified-from-source)
Age-bias corrected metrics indicate high accuracy even for poorly performing models (shuffled-label experiments) (verified-from-source)
The label-free slope correction (divide by slope, Cole et al. 2018) inflates variance in the data (verified-from-source)
r and R2 are lower in samples with a narrower target range; MAE/RMSE fall with a narrower range (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: Do not stretch CV/HEX predictions to match the label spread: for a calibrated predictor the prediction/label SD ratio equals r (0.686 vs our observed 0.66, our derivation), so the compression is expected; any de-shrink factor must be fitted on OOF MAPE, and the 'outer deciles' diagnostic (binned by true label) will always look bad.

has_limitation.note: Corrected metrics can hide low prediction variance; recommend inspecting uncorrected results
Does not evaluate label-free corrections on held-out MAE, so the cost of variance inflation is argued, not measured

nodes.title: Mean Absolute Percentage Error for regression models
nodes.citation: de Myttenaere A, Golden B, Le Grand B, Rossi F. Mean Absolute Percentage Error for regression models. Neurocomputing. 2016;192:38-48. doi:10.1016/j.neucom.2015.12.114
nodes.tldr: Proves that minimising MAPE is weighted MAE regression with weights 1/|y|, that a MAPE-optimal model exists and that MAPE empirical risk minimisation is universally consistent; the MAPE-optimal estimate sits below the conditional median.
nodes.relevance_note: Our score is per-metric MAPE, so the loss to train/decode is MAE weighted by 1/y, and the optimal point is a 1/y-weighted median, not the mean or median.
nodes.data_scale: theory + 1-D simulation (1000 train / 1000 test points)
key_numbers: Minimising MAPE is equivalent to weighted MAE regression with sample weights 1/|y_i| (verified-from-source)
Kernel version = weighted quantile (pinball) regression with weights 1/|y_i| (verified-from-source)
Consistency proof requires |Y| >= Y_L > 0 almost surely (labels bounded away from zero) (verified-from-source)
Simulation: 1000 training and 1000 test points, Gaussian kernel, C chosen by 5-fold CV (verified-from-source)
MAPE-trained model clearly beats MAE-trained model only when targets are near zero; for targets far from zero the two tie (verified-from-source)

results.value: lower than MAE-model only for small offsets a

nodes.suggests_try: Train or post-hoc decode each metric with 1/y-weighted L1 (or 1/y-weighted median over an ensemble / predicted distribution) instead of MSE/plain L1; expected gain is small for CD (labels far from zero, low relative noise) and largest where relative label spread is big (CV 0.29-0.50).

has_limitation.note: Consistency needs labels bounded away from zero; regularised ERM consistency left open
Only a 1-D simulation; no deep networks, no label noise model

nodes.title: Corneal endothelium evaluation with 2 noncontact specular microscopes and their semiautomated methods of analysis
nodes.citation: de Sanctis U, Machetta F, Razzano L, Dalmasso P, Grignolo FM. Corneal endothelium evaluation with 2 noncontact specular microscopes and their semiautomated methods of analysis. Cornea. 2006;25(5):501-506. doi:10.1097/01.ico.0000214217.83119.af
nodes.tldr: In 49 normal subjects, two examiners using the Topcon SP-2000P retraced method and the Konan CC7000 center method agreed well on cell size and density (ICC > 0.85) but poorly on CV and hexagonality (ICC < 0.65), and CV/HEX correlated at r < 0.20 between the two instruments.
nodes.relevance_note: Quantifies how much of CV/HEX is reader and device behaviour rather than biology; supports treating CV/HEX labels as heavily noisy.
nodes.data_scale: 49 normal subjects, 2 examiners, 2 instruments
key_numbers: Inter-examiner ICC > 0.85 for average cell size and ECD (from-abstract)
Inter-examiner ICC < 0.65 for CV and hexagonality (from-abstract)
Topcon vs Konan ECD mean difference -184 (examiner 1) and -228 cells/mm2 (examiner 2) (from-abstract)
CV and HEX between instruments: no mean difference (P > 0.05) but r < 0.20 (from-abstract)
nodes.suggests_try: Use these reliabilities to set realistic targets: if reader ICC for CV/HEX is below 0.65 in normal eyes, a model at CV r 0.69 is near the reader ceiling, so spend remaining time on loss/decoding (MAPE-optimal shrinkage, noise-aware heads) rather than on better cell finding.
search_keywords: interexaminer reproducibility specular microscopy CV hexagonality

has_limitation.note: Normal eyes only (narrow CV/HEX range lowers ICC/r mechanically); abstract-level read; old devices.

nodes.title: On the regional variability of averaged cell area estimates for the human corneal endothelium in relation to the extent of polymegethism
nodes.citation: Doughty MJ. On the regional variability of averaged cell area estimates for the human corneal endothelium in relation to the extent of polymegethism. Int Ophthalmol. 2018;38(6):2537-2546 (online 2017). doi:10.1007/s10792-017-0765-2
nodes.tldr: Hand-traced areas of 200 cells in each of 80 Topcon SP-3000P images show that mean cell area is stable across 20-cell blocks, but COV of cell area becomes unreliable with 50 or fewer cells in polymegethous endothelium (can differ by +/-10 % or more); at least 75-100 contiguous cells are recommended.
nodes.relevance_note: Quantifies how much CV (and much less mean area/CD) depends on which and how many cells are sampled; directly bears on label noise from the ~150-cell technician-chosen region and on the expected CV floor.
nodes.data_scale: 80 central Topcon SP-3000P images (4 groups of 20 by global COV), 200 hand-traced cells each (16,000 cells)
key_numbers: Pooled 16,000 cells: mean area 421 um2; 20-cell block means within +/-14 um2 of the overall mean; SD of block means about 70 um2 (verified-from-source)
With <= 50 cells in moderate-to-marked polymegethism, global COV could differ by +/-10 % or more (verified-from-source)
Recommended: 75-100 contiguous cells per image, at least about 100 for reliable estimates (verified-from-source)
Manually traced global COV spans <30 % (uniform) to >50-60 % (marked) on Topcon SP-3000P images (verified-from-source)
Uniform endothelium (COV < 30 %): COV variability drops beyond 120 cells (6 blocks) (verified-from-source)

results.task: COV stability vs number of sampled cells
results.dataset: 80 Topcon SP-3000P images, 200 traced cells each

nodes.suggests_try: Model label noise as heteroscedastic: CV label noise grows with the label's own CV (polymegethous frames vary more by region), so weight CV loss by 1/(expected sampling variance) or use a noise-aware loss, and do not chase the outer CV deciles with heavy per-sample weighting beyond what this sampling noise allows.

has_limitation.note: Single observer; analysis possibly statistical overkill
Sequential contiguous blocks, not random sampling; groups defined by the outcome variable; abstract and results disagree on whether >100 cells helps in marked polymegethism

nodes.title: Importance of standardizing the number of cells measured for coefficient of variation (COV) estimates of corneal endothelial cell area values as relevant to contact lens wear
nodes.citation: Doughty MJ. Importance of standardizing the number of cells measured for coefficient of variation (COV) estimates of corneal endothelial cell area values as relevant to contact lens wear. Cont Lens Anterior Eye. 2020;44(3):101336. doi:10.1016/j.clae.2020.05.005
nodes.tldr: CV estimates from manually measured cell areas stabilise only near 90 cells and their uncertainty grows with polymegethism (about +-1 % at CV 26 % to +-5 % at CV 57 %, relative to the >100-cell value); the number of cells should be the same across a data set.
nodes.relevance_note: Gives the shape of CV label noise: it scales with the CV itself and with fewer cells, so CV label noise is heteroscedastic (larger in the upper CV decile).
nodes.data_scale: 4 sets x 20 non-contact specular images, graded by polymegethism (grade 0-3)
key_numbers: Group-mean COV 25.8, 33.1, 45.1, 56.8 % for grades 0-3 (from-abstract)
Reliability with 90 cells: about +-1.0, +-2.7, +-3.6, +-5.0 % (relative to the >100-cell value) (from-abstract)
Reliability with 75 cells: +-3.4, +-5.3, +-6.1, +-7.9 % (from-abstract)
Recommendation: 75-100 cells per image, same number across the data set (from-abstract)

nodes.title: Segmentation of corneal endothelium images using a U-Net-based convolutional neural network
nodes.citation: Fabijanska A. Segmentation of corneal endothelium images using a U-Net-based convolutional neural network. Artif Intell Med. 2018;88:1-13. doi:10.1016/j.artmed.2018.04.004
nodes.tldr: U-Net edge probability + binarisation + skeletonisation on 30 specular images: DICE 0.86, cell-count MAPE 4.5 %, but morphometric errors of 5.2 % (ECD), 6.2 % (HEX) and 11.93 % (CV), showing CV amplifies small segmentation errors the most.
nodes.relevance_note: Clean dose-response: a 4.5 % cell-count error already gives about 12 % CV error, close to our CV MAPE (10.11); supports not building CV on imperfect masks.
nodes.data_scale: 30 corneal endothelium specular images (15 train / 15 test per later papers)
key_numbers: AUROC 0.92 for border pixels; DICE 0.86 on average (from-abstract)
Cell-number MAPE 4.5 % (from-abstract)
Morphometric errors: ECD 5.2 %, hexagonality 6.2 %, CV of cell size 11.93 % (from-abstract)

has_limitation.note: 30 images only; abstract-level reading; ground truth manual edges, not device values

nodes.title: Stop Regressing: Training Value Functions via Classification for Scalable Deep RL
nodes.venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 235
nodes.citation: Farebrother J, Orbay J, Vuong Q, Taïga AA, Chebotar Y, Xiao T, et al. Stop Regressing: Training Value Functions via Classification for Scalable Deep RL. Proceedings of ICML 2024, PMLR 235:13049-13071. arXiv:2403.03950
nodes.tldr: Replacing MSE regression with cross-entropy on a histogram whose target is a Gaussian-smoothed bin distribution (HL-Gauss, sigma/bin = 0.75) consistently improves deep value-function learning and degrades more gracefully than MSE under noisy targets.
nodes.relevance_note: Our CV labels are already discrete (step 0.01, 78 values) and noisy; an HL-Gauss head with sigma set to the known label noise gives a full predictive distribution we can decode for MAPE.
nodes.data_scale: Atari 2600 (single and multi-task), robotic manipulation, chess, Wordle (RL)
key_numbers: HL-Gauss: target = Gaussian (mean = scalar target, std sigma) integrated over each bin; default sigma/bin-width = 0.75, spreading mass to about 6 bins; decode = expectation (verified-from-source)
About 30 % IQM improvement with SoftMoE scaling on single-task Atari (verified-from-source)
With reward noise eta in {0.1, 0.3, 1.0}, HL-Gauss degrades more gracefully than MSE; no numbers given in text (verified-from-source)
HL-Gauss substantially outperforms Two-Hot and MSE losses on online Atari (verified-from-source)
Gain over MSE largely disappears in offline SARSA, so part of the benefit is handling non-stationary targets (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: Swap the CV (and HEX) regression head for a histogram head: 78+ bins at step 0.01 for CV, HL-Gauss targets with sigma about 2-3 bins (close to the 6.5 % label SE at CV 0.38), trained with cross-entropy; decode the 1/y-weighted median per image rather than the expectation, and compare OOF MAPE against the current head.

compares_with.note: both find classification heads beat MSE; Farebrother adds Gaussian smoothing and noise robustness

has_limitation.note: Benefit partly tied to non-stationary RL targets; smaller under stationary (offline SARSA) targets

nodes.title: Deep Label Distribution Learning With Label Ambiguity
nodes.citation: Gao BB, Xing C, Xie CW, Wu J, Geng X. Deep Label Distribution Learning With Label Ambiguity. IEEE Trans Image Process. 2017;26(6):2825-2838. doi:10.1109/TIP.2017.2689998
nodes.tldr: Replace each scalar/ordinal label with a discretised Gaussian over neighbouring label values (sigma = known label ambiguity, e.g. annotator std) and train with KL divergence; beats L2/L1 regression and plain classification on age and head-pose estimation.
nodes.relevance_note: Our CV/HEX labels are discrete and carry a known, computable sampling spread from about 150 cells; DLDL is the recipe for encoding that spread as the training target.
nodes.data_scale: Morph, ChaLearn LAP apparent age; Pointing'04, BJUT-3D, AFLW head pose; VOC2007 multi-label; VOC2011 segmentation
key_numbers: Target y_j = normalised Gaussian p(l_j | mu, sigma) over discrete labels; loss = KL (cross-entropy) to softmax; decode by expectation or argmax (verified-from-source)
Morph age MAE: DLDL 2.52 vs L2 regression 3.17 vs L1 regression 2.88 vs softmax classification 2.86 (verified-from-source)
ChaLearn age MAE / epsilon-error: DLDL 5.34/0.44 vs L1 regression 5.62/0.47 vs classification 7.95/0.58 (verified-from-source)
sigma = 2 years fixed on Morph (no per-image ambiguity given); ChaLearn provides per-image apparent-age std (verified-from-source)
MAE vs sigma is V-shaped; authors suggest sigma near the spacing between neighbouring labels, tuned by CV (verified-from-source)

nodes.title: Comparison of corneal endothelial cell measurements by two non-contact specular microscopes
nodes.citation: Gasser L, Reinhard T, Böhringer D. Comparison of corneal endothelial cell measurements by two non-contact specular microscopes. BMC Ophthalmol. 2015;15:87. doi:10.1186/s12886-015-0068-1
nodes.tldr: With cells marked manually by one examiner on both devices, the Konan Noncon Robo SP8000 read ECD 187 cells/mm2 (9.6 %) higher and CV 8 points higher (37 vs 29) than the Topcon SP3000P on the same 34 eyes; CV and HEX correlated only weakly between devices.
nodes.relevance_note: Direct evidence that the CV scale is set by the device's own polygon construction, not by the cells; our labels (likely Konan) and the external Topcon point set live on different CV scales.
nodes.data_scale: 34 eyes of 18 patients; Konan 110 +- 45 and Topcon 100 +- 30 cells per measurement

nodes.title: Making and evaluating point forecasts
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
nodes.citation: Gneiting T. Making and evaluating point forecasts. J Am Stat Assoc. 2011;106(494):746-762. doi:10.1198/jasa.2011.r10138
nodes.tldr: Point forecasts must match the scoring function: squared error elicits the mean, absolute error the median, and absolute percentage error elicits the 'median of order -1' (median of the density proportional to f(y)/y); mismatched scoring can rank a skilled forecaster below a biased one.
nodes.relevance_note: Tells us exactly which summary of a predictive distribution to submit under per-metric MAPE: med^(-1), the median of f(y)/y, which lies below the median.
nodes.data_scale: theory + simulation (n = 100,000)
key_numbers: APE |(x-y)/y| is consistent for the median of order -1, med^(-1), i.e. the median of the density proportional to y^(-1) f(y) (verified-from-source)
Relative error |(x-y)/x| is consistent for the median of order +1, med^(1) (verified-from-source)
Squared error is consistent for the mean; a score is mean-consistent iff it is a Bregman function (Savage 1971) (verified-from-source)
Simulation n = 100,000: the 'pessimist' gets the best AE and APE and the 'optimist' the best RE, although the 'statistician' is the most skilled by construction (verified-from-source)
Simulated APE: statistician 2.58e5 vs pessimist 0.14e5 vs Bayes rule 1.00 (epsilon forecast) (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: Predict a distribution per metric (histogram head or ensemble) and submit med^(-1) = the 1/y-weighted median, not the mean; for a log-normal predictive with log-sd s this equals median*exp(-s^2) (our derivation), i.e. about 2 % below the median at s = 0.15.

has_limitation.note: med^(-1) may not exist for heavy-tailed or near-zero positive variables; then optimal APE forecast tends to zero

nodes.title: Is the Performance of My Deep Network Too Good to Be True? A Direct Approach to Estimating the Bayes Error in Binary Classification
nodes.citation: Ishida T, Yamane I, Charoenphakdee N, Niu G, Sugiyama M. Is the Performance of My Deep Network Too Good to Be True? A Direct Approach to Estimating the Bayes Error in Binary Classification. ICLR 2023. arXiv:2202.00395
nodes.tldr: The Bayes (irreducible) error can be estimated without any model by averaging min(c, 1-c) over soft labels c = p(y=1|x); with noisy soft labels the naive estimate is biased and needs correction; ViT already reaches the estimated floor on CIFAR-10H.
nodes.relevance_note: The principle (estimate the floor from the label-generating noise, not from models) is what we need to judge how far CV/HEX/CD OOF error sits above the irreducible label-noise floor; the method itself is binary-classification only.
nodes.data_scale: CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H (new), ICLR 2017-2023 review scores
key_numbers: Estimator: mean of min(c_i, 1 - c_i) over clean soft labels; unbiased, consistent, O_P(1/sqrt(n)) (verified-from-source)
Noisy soft labels: naive estimator is biased and the bias does not vanish with n (Theorem 3.3); corrected with sign labels (verified-from-source)
Fashion-MNIST-H: estimated Bayes error 3.478 % (95 % CI +-0.079) vs ResNet-18 test error 3.852 % (SE +-0.041) (verified-from-source)
CIFAR-10H: ViT B/16 error at or slightly above the estimated Bayes error after adjusting for the label distribution (verified-from-source)
ICLR accept/reject Bayes error estimates 6.8 % (2017) to 9.6 % (2022) (verified-from-source)
No regression extension in the paper (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: Regression analogue for us (our derivation): floor MAPE = E|label - truth|/label from the sampling model alone; for Gaussian relative noise with SE 6.5 % (CV), 7.5 % (HEX), 3 % (CD) that is about 0.8 x SE = 5.2, 6.0, 2.4; compare with OOF 10.11 / 9.74 / 6.19 to bound what any device-behaviour model could still gain, and note that, like the paper's noisy soft labels, a floor from an uncertain noise model is itself biased.

has_limitation.note: Naive estimator biased under noisy soft labels; human-label distributions may inflate the estimate
Binary classification only; regression floors need a noise model such as our cell-sampling model

nodes.title: What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision?
nodes.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017)
nodes.citation: Kendall A, Gal Y. What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision? Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017). 2017:5574-5584. arXiv:1703.04977
nodes.tldr: Heteroscedastic regression loss 0.5*exp(-s)*||y - f||^2 + 0.5*s (s = predicted log-variance) lets the network attenuate the loss on noisy targets; it gives small gains on depth regression and segmentation, and aleatoric variance does not shrink with more data.
nodes.relevance_note: Gives a per-image predicted noise level, which both down-weights noisy labels in training and tells us how far to shift each prediction toward the MAPE-optimal point (median of order -1).

CamVid IoU: baseline 67.1 vs +aleatoric 67.4 vs +both 67.5 (verified-from-source)

nodes.title: Stochastic Order Learning: An Approach to Rank Estimation Using Noisy Data
nodes.venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026 (accepted; arXiv)
nodes.citation: Lee C, Lee SH, Kim CS. Stochastic Order Learning: An Approach to Rank Estimation Using Noisy Data. ICML 2026 (accepted). arXiv:2607.08103
nodes.tldr: Treats each noisy ordinal label as a discrete-Gaussian distribution over plausible true ranks and trains rank centroids with a discriminative loss plus a probabilistic pairwise order loss; best or near-best MAE on noisy age, aesthetics, bone-age and MT-score benchmarks, ahead of noisy-regression methods (ConFrag, C-Mixup).
nodes.relevance_note: Most recent method built for exactly our label type: discrete ordered targets with zero-mean noise of known shape (CV step 0.01, about 6.5 % sampling noise); also a medical regression benchmark (RSNA bone age).
nodes.data_scale: MORPH II, CLAP2015 (age), AADB (aesthetics), RSNA (bone age), WMT2020 (MT quality scores)
key_numbers: Noise model: zero-mean discrete Gaussian over neighbouring ranks; synthetic levels kappa 0.2-0.4 (age), 0.1-0.2 (RSNA); Laplacian, uniform, skewed variants also tested (verified-from-source)
CLAP2015, Gaussian kappa 0.4, MAE/CS: SOL 4.002/73.68 vs GOL 4.105/72.10 vs ConFrag 5.328/58.20 vs C-Mixup 5.302/58.52 (verified-from-source)
MORPH II, kappa 0.4: SOL 2.826 vs MWR 2.851 vs GOL 2.861 MAE (verified-from-source)
RSNA bone age, kappa 0.1: SOL 7.579 vs MWR 7.833 vs GOL 8.170 MAE (verified-from-source)
Ablation CLAP2015 kappa 0.3: order loss alone 3.785, discriminative loss alone 16.433, full 3.764 MAE (verified-from-source)
Real noise WMT2020: PCC 0.680 vs 0.660 for best prior (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: The cheap transferable part is the pairwise order loss weighted by the probability that label i truly exceeds label j under the known noise (Gaussian with SE about 6.5 % on CV): add it to the CV head on frozen features (pairs within a batch) so near-tied pairs carry no gradient while far-apart pairs enforce order; judge by OOF MAPE and prediction spread.

has_limitation.note: Discrete Gaussian error model chosen for tractability; not best everywhere (RSNA under Laplacian noise)

nodes.title: Data augmentation via warping transforms for modeling natural variability in the corneal endothelium enhances semi-supervised segmentation

nodes.title: A Method for Auto-Differentiation of the Voronoi Tessellation
nodes.citation: Shumilin S, Ryabov A, Barannikov S, Burnaev E, Vanovskii V. A Method for Auto-Differentiation of the Voronoi Tessellation. arXiv:2312.16192 (v3, 2024)
nodes.tldr: Makes 2-D Voronoi cell areas, edge lengths and vertex positions differentiable with respect to site coordinates (circumcentre formulas + shoelace areas in PyTorch); adjacency comes from a non-differentiable Delaunay step, so topology is fixed between retriangulations.
nodes.relevance_note: The building block for a 'differentiable cell-graph head' (points -> Voronoi -> area CV) supervised by image-level CV, but it can only move points, not add or delete them, and neighbour counts (HEX) are not differentiable.

Area-variance minimisation with 1000 points, 1400 Adam steps at lr 0.001, variance converges almost to zero (qualitative only) (verified-from-source)

nodes.title: Aleatoric uncertainty estimation with test-time augmentation for medical image segmentation with convolutional neural networks
nodes.citation: Wang G, Li W, Aertsen M, Deprest J, Ourselin S, Vercauteren T. Aleatoric uncertainty estimation with test-time augmentation for medical image segmentation with convolutional neural networks. Neurocomputing. 2019;338:34-45. doi:10.1016/j.neucom.2019.01.103

nodes.title: Domain Generalization for Medical Image Analysis: A Review
nodes.citation: Yoon JS, Oh K, Shin Y, Mazurowski MA, Suk HI. Domain Generalization for Medical Image Analysis: A Review. arXiv:2310.08598 (v3, Dec 2024)
nodes.tldr: Workflow-oriented review of domain generalisation in medical imaging with a data-level / feature-level / model-level / analysis-level taxonomy; no quantitative benchmark, no regression tasks; notes histogram matching scored best among common DG methods in one cited benchmark and lists intensity normalisation, augmentation and ensembles as data/model-level tools.
nodes.relevance_note: Map of options for our two-source acquisition shift; it confirms that data-level methods (normalisation, augmentation) are the efficient first step, but offers no regression-specific or quantitative guidance.
nodes.data_scale: Review; 1,621 papers in its database
key_numbers: Taxonomy: data-level, feature-level, model-level, analysis-level (verified-from-source)
Cites a benchmark where histogram matching had the highest performance among some commonly used DG methods (verified-from-source)
No quantitative comparison table; regression tasks not discussed (verified-from-source)
nodes.suggests_try: As a cheap baseline for the darker 2023-24 frames, test histogram matching of each image to a reference intensity histogram from the other source (alongside flat-field correction and augmentation) and compare per-source MAPE.
search_keywords: domain generalization medical image analysis review

has_limitation.note: Benchmarks for DG need expansion; source-limited and concept-shift settings remain open
No numbers to choose between methods; TTA treated only as a related task

nodes.title: Generalizing Deep Learning for Medical Image Segmentation to Unseen Domains via Deep Stacked Transformation
nodes.citation: Zhang L, Wang X, Yang D, Roth H, Myronenko A, Xu D, et al. Generalizing Deep Learning for Medical Image Segmentation to Unseen Domains via Deep Stacked Transformation. IEEE Trans Med Imaging. 2020;39(7):2531-2540. doi:10.1109/TMI.2020.2973595
nodes.tldr: BigAug stacks nine augmentations (blur, sharpen, noise, brightness, contrast/gamma, intensity perturbation, rotation, scaling, deformation; each p=0.5) on single-source training and raises unseen-domain Dice from 49.8 to 80.0 on average, beating CycleGAN adaptation (63.5); sharpening, brightness and contrast mattered most for MRI.
nodes.relevance_note: Cheapest proven defence against acquisition shift without target data; directly applicable to our darker, vignetted 2023-24 source and to the HEX OOF-to-test gap, and costs nothing at inference.
nodes.data_scale: Prostate MRI (source MSD-P 26/6; unseen PROMISE12 50, NCI-ISBI13 60, ProstateX 98), left atrium MRI (MSD-H 16/4; ASC 100, MM-WHS 20), LV ultrasound (CETUS-A 8/2; CETUS-B/C 10 each); large-data 465-volume MRI source
key_numbers: Unseen-domain average Dice: baseline 49.8, CycleGAN adaptation 63.5, top-4 augmentations 74.9, BigAug 80.0, supervised reference 91.5 (verified-from-source)
Source-domain Dice also rises: 89.1 baseline -> 91.6 BigAug (verified-from-source)
Single-transform ablation, unseen avg Dice: brightness 63.6, contrast 63.6, sharpening 62.9, blur 61.1, scaling 61.3, rotation 54.7, deformation 51.1 (verified-from-source)
Large data (465 volumes): unseen average 89.6 BigAug vs 87.5 baseline (verified-from-source)
Ranges: blur sigma 0.25-1.5, noise sigma 0.1-1.0, brightness +-0.1, gamma 0.5-1.0 or 1.0-4.5, scaling 0.4-1.6, rotation +-20 deg (verified-from-source)
